claim: Viruses are the most abundant biological entities in the biosphere.
source: Viruses are the most abundant biological entities in the biosphere (Baltimore, 1971; Suttle, 2005; Suttle, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Baltimore, 1971; Suttle, 2005; Suttle, 2007

claim: Active energy metabolism pathways and the autonomous ability to reproduce independently are the most fundamental criteria associated with living cells.
source: Active energy metabolism pathways and the autonomous ability to reproduce independently are the most fundamental criteria associated with living cells and therefore distinguish the three domains of life – archaea, bacteria, and eukarya – from viral entities.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of what defines living organisms

claim: The fundamental hallmark of all living organisms is the self-maintenance of their own functional and structural integrity via the biochemical transformations of environmental resources.
source: Specifically, the fundamental hallmark of all living organisms is the self-maintenance of their own functional and structural integrity via the biochemical transformations of environmental resources. (Dupré and O'Malley, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupré and O'Malley, 2009

claim: Viruses were originally defined as filterable agents capable of passing through membrane filters with pore sizes of 0.22 µm.
source: Viruses originally were defined as filterable agents capable of passing through membrane filters with pore sizes of 0.22 µm.
evidence: Based on historical scientific definition of viruses

claim: Most viruses possess small genomes that carry only a handful of genes supporting their replication and capsid production in a host cell.
source: Most viruses possess small genomes that carry only a handful of genes supporting their replication and capsid production in a host cell.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about typical virus characteristics

claim: Viruses have been characterized as 'molecular genetic parasites' that take advantage of cellular functions to replicate.
source: Viruses have thus been characterized as 'molecular genetic parasites' that take advantage of cellular functions to replicate (Luria, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luria, 1959

claim: Viruses hijack the host cellular metabolic pathways to their own advantage with the ultimate goal to replicate.
source: Generally, once viruses find their replication site they hijack the host cellular metabolic pathways to their own advantage with the ultimate goal to replicate (Villarreal, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Villarreal, 2005

claim: A 'virocell' is defined as a 'living form' of the virus, consisting of a living cell transformed to produce more virions.
source: However, ambiguity regarding the definition of viruses appears in the concept of a 'virocell', defined by Forterre, 2013 as a 'living form' of the virus, consisting of a living cell transformed to produce more virions (Forterre, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forterre, 2013

claim: Intracellular bacteria such as Rickettsia and Chlamydia hijack host energy metabolism enabling their persistence and proliferation.
source: At the blurred boundaries between viruses and cellular organisms, intracellular bacteria such as Rickettsia and Chlamydia also are known to hijack host energy metabolism enabling their persistence and proliferation (Driscoll et al., 2017; Gehre, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Driscoll et al., 2017; Gehre, 2015

claim: Viruses lack many of the essential attributes of living organisms, such as the ability to capture and store free energy, as well as autonomous replication and self-repairing capacity.
source: Ultimately, however, viruses lack many of the essential attributes of living organisms, such as the ability to capture and store free energy, as well as autonomous replication and self-repairing capacity (Dupré and O'Malley, 2009; Regenmortel, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dupré and O'Malley, 2009; Regenmortel, 2010

claim: The discovery of giant viruses of amoeba in 2003 revolutionized the view of viruses.
source: In 2003, the discovery of the giant viruses of amoeba revolutionized the view of viruses (La Scola et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to La Scola et al., 2003

claim: Giant virus particles can reach up to 2.5 μm in size.
source: Specifically, the size of the giant virus particles (reaching up to 2.5 μm) and of their genome sizes (up to 2.5 Mb), encoding almost a thousand proteins, fundamentally changed the landscape of virus research (Philippe et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Philippe et al., 2013

claim: Giant virus genomes can reach up to 2.5 Mb in size and encode almost a thousand proteins.
source: Specifically, the size of the giant virus particles (reaching up to 2.5 μm) and of their genome sizes (up to 2.5 Mb), encoding almost a thousand proteins, fundamentally changed the landscape of virus research (Philippe et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Philippe et al., 2013

claim: Acanthamoeba polyphaga Mimivirus has a 1.2-Mbp genome.
source: Notably, Acanthamoeba polyphaga Mimivirus, the first giant virus of amoeba discovered, has a 1.2-Mbp genome, and possesses several genes encoding proteins involved in transcription and translation (Raoult et al., 2004; Raoult and Forterre, 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Raoult et al., 2004; Raoult and Forterre, 2008b

claim: Acanthamoeba polyphaga Mimivirus possesses several genes encoding proteins involved in transcription and translation.
source: Notably, Acanthamoeba polyphaga Mimivirus, the first giant virus of amoeba discovered, has a 1.2-Mbp genome, and possesses several genes encoding proteins involved in transcription and translation (Raoult et al., 2004; Raoult and Forterre, 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Raoult et al., 2004; Raoult and Forterre, 2008b

claim: Some bacterial and eukaryotic genes found in the Mimivirus genome were acquired by horizontal gene transfer from amoebal hosts and from amoebal bacteria parasites.
source: Phylogenetic analyses have demonstrated that some bacterial and eukaryotic genes found in the Mimivirus genome, and other giant virus genomes, were acquired by horizontal gene transfer from amoebal hosts, and from amoebal bacteria parasites (Moreira and Brochier-Armanet, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moreira and Brochier-Armanet, 2008

claim: Most giant virus genes have enigmatic origins.
source: Phylogenetic analyses have demonstrated that some bacterial and eukaryotic genes found in the Mimivirus genome, and other giant virus genomes, were acquired by horizontal gene transfer from amoebal hosts, and from amoebal bacteria parasites (Moreira and Brochier-Armanet, 2008), although most giant virus genes still have enigmatic origins.
evidence: Stated as a fact following discussion of horizontal gene transfer

claim: Giant viruses represent a group of ancient viruses termed the Nucleo–Cytoplasmic Large DNA Viruses (NCLDVs).
source: Giant viruses represent a group of ancient viruses that are termed the Nucleo–Cytoplasmic Large DNA Viruses (NCLDVs).
evidence: Based on established taxonomic classification

claim: NCLDVs infect hosts ranging from algae to animals and form an apparently monophyletic group in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota.
source: While some are found in amoebae, other of these viruses infect hosts ranging from algae to animals and form an apparently monophyletic group in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota (Colson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colson et al., 2013

claim: Giant viruses are classified into several families: Mimiviridae, Pithoviridae, Pandoraviridae, Phycodnaviridae, Poxviridae, Iridoviridae, Asfarviridae, and others.
source: The giant viruses are classified into several families: Mimiviridae, Pithoviridae, Pandoraviridae, Phycodnaviridae, Poxviridae, Iridoviridae, Asfarviridae, and others.
evidence: Based on established taxonomic classification

claim: Many newly discovered viruses in the Mollivirus genus are not yet classified.
source: Many, including newly discovered viruses in the Mollivirus genus are not yet classified (Abergel et al., 2015; Legendre et al., 2014; Rolland et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abergel et al., 2015; Legendre et al., 2014; Rolland et al., 2019

claim: Giant virus genomes encode proteins that had never before been identified in viruses.
source: The genomes of giant viruses encode proteins that had never before been identified in viruses.
evidence: Based on comparison with previously known viral proteins

claim: Giant virus proteins have sequence identity with closely related eukaryotic homologs.
source: These proteins have sequence identity with closely related eukaryotic homologs (Chelkha et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chelkha et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020

claim: Cafeteria roenbergensis virus, Klosneuviruses and Tupanviruses encode several gene products that are involved in protein translation.
source: For example, Cafeteria roenbergensis virus, Klosneuviruses and Tupanviruses encode several gene products that are involved in protein translation (Abrahão et al., 2018; Schulz et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Abrahão et al., 2018; Schulz et al., 2017

claim: The presence of translation machinery had not been previously described in viruses before the discovery in Cafeteria roenbergensis virus, Klosneuviruses and Tupanviruses.
source: For example, Cafeteria roenbergensis virus, Klosneuviruses and Tupanviruses encode several gene products that are involved in protein translation (Abrahão et al., 2018; Schulz et al., 2017); the presence of such translation machinery had not been previously described in viruses.
evidence: Based on historical knowledge of viral characteristics

claim: The presence of translation machinery in some giant viruses suggests that those viruses may have relative independence from their hosts.
source: This finding suggested that those viruses may have relative independence from their hosts (and hence are 'quasi-autonomous' viruses) (Claverie and Abergel, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Claverie and Abergel, 2010, and logical inference from the presence of translation machinery

claim: Giant virus gene products have been implicated in RNA maturation, DNA maintenance, and proteostasis.
source: In addition to the translation components, giant virus gene products have been implicated in RNA maturation, DNA maintenance, and proteostasis (Fischer et al., 2010; Yutin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2010; Yutin et al., 2013

claim: Metabolic genes involved in specialized cellular biochemical pathways have been discovered in some giant viruses.
source: Recently, defined metabolic genes involved in specialized cellular biochemical pathways have also been discovered in some giant viruses (Aherfi et al., 2022; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Schulz et al., 2020; Schvarcz and Steward, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aherfi et al., 2022; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Schulz et al., 2020; Schvarcz and Steward, 2018

claim: Carbohydrates are key enzymatic substrates for many essential metabolic pathways in cells.
source: Carbohydrates are key enzymatic substrates for many essential metabolic pathways in cells (Maughan, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maughan, 2009

claim: Autotrophic organisms biosynthesize carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water via photosynthesis.
source: Generally, autotrophic organisms biosynthesize carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, via photosynthesis (Butterworth, 2005; Lehninger et al., 2004; Nelson and Cox, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Butterworth, 2005; Lehninger et al., 2004; Nelson and Cox, 2017

claim: All organisms break down stored or consumed carbohydrates in order to produce energy for cell functioning.
source: All organisms then break down stored or consumed carbohydrates in order to produce energy for cell functioning (Nelson and Cox, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nelson and Cox, 2017

claim: Both autotrophic and heterotrophic organisms temporarily store their generated energy in the form of high-energy molecules such as ATP and NADH.
source: Both autotrophic and heterotrophic organisms temporarily store their generated energy in the form of high-energy molecules, for example adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), for use in the various metabolic processes (Sanders, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanders, 2016

claim: Auxiliary metabolic genes encoded by giant viruses appear to exercise control and modulation of host cellular energetic metabolism, especially during viral genome replication, gene expression, and virion assembly.
source: Although some viruses in the Nucleocytoviricota phylum infect known hosts such as amoeba, it is not clear if these are actually the specific hosts. In any case, auxiliary metabolic genes (AMG) encoded by giant viruses appear to exercise control and modulation of host cellular energetic metabolism, especially during viral genome replication, gene expression, and virion assembly (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2020

claim: Control mechanisms of host metabolism by giant viruses can be based on transcriptional regulation of nuclear and mitochondrion-encoded genes that are involved in energy metabolism, as observed with coccolithoviruses.
source: Such control mechanisms can be based on transcriptional regulation of nuclear and mitochondrion-encoded genes that are involved in energy metabolism, as observed with coccolithoviruses (Ku et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ku et al., 2020

claim: Single cell transcriptomics of Emiliania huxleyi during infection by its specific giant virus showed that either host or viral transcriptome dominated the generated mRNA pool.
source: Single cell transcriptomics of the microalga Emiliania huxleyi during infection by its specific giant virus showed that either host or viral transcriptome dominated the generated mRNA pool, and that only very few cells were observed in intermediate states.
evidence: Based on single cell transcriptomics data

claim: The rapid shutdown of host transcript generation indicates that the E. huxleyi coccolithovirus massively takes over controlling synthesis of almost the entire mRNA pool.
source: The rapid shutdown of host transcript generation indicates that the E. huxleyi coccolithovirus massively takes over controlling synthesis of almost the entire mRNA pool.
evidence: Inferred from single cell transcriptomics data showing rapid shutdown

claim: Many giant viral genes and gene products related to energy production and metabolic pathways have been identified recently.
source: Many giant viral genes and gene products related to energy production and metabolic pathways have been identified recently (Aherfi et al., 2022; Ha et al., 2021; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aherfi et al., 2022; Ha et al., 2021; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020 and Figure 1

claim: In a database of 2436 annotated Nucleocytoviricota, hundreds of viruses, mainly from the Mimiviridae and Phycodnaviridae families, were identified with expressed viral transcripts that are genes involved in glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the TCA cycle, and the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: In a detailed study examining a database of 2436 annotated Nucleocytoviricota, including metatranscriptomic data from California's surface waters, hundreds of viruses, mainly from the Mimiviridae and Phycodnaviridae families, were identified. Many expressed viral transcripts in this dataset are genes involved in glycolysis (e.g. phosphofructokinase [EC 2.7.1.11], glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase [EC 1.2. 1.12], phosphoglycerate mutase [EC 5.4.2.11]), gluconeogenesis (e.g. phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase [EC 4.1.1.32] and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase [EC 3.1.3.11]), the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (e.g. succinate dehydrogenase [EC 1.3.5.1]), and the pentose phosphate pathway (e.g. 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase EC 1.1.1.1; Ha et al., 2021; Ha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ha et al., 2021 and based on database analysis

claim: Glycolysis is an ancient metabolic pathway that occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and converts glucose into pyruvate.
source: Glycolysis is an ancient metabolic pathway that occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and converts glucose into pyruvate, which is accompanied by transfer of electrons to NAD+ in order to generate NADH2 (Potter and Fothergill-Gilmore, 1993; Kumari, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Potter and Fothergill-Gilmore, 1993; Kumari, 2018

claim: Gluconeogenesis is a process occurring in animals, fungi, plants, and bacteria, which results in the generation of glucose from non-carbohydrate carbon substrates such as lactate, amino acids, and glycerol.
source: Inversely, gluconeogenesis is a process occurring in animals, fungi, plants, and bacteria, which results in the generation of glucose from non-carbohydrate carbon substrates such as lactate, amino acids, and glycerol (Rodwell et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodwell et al., 2015

claim: Genes encoding the glycolytic enzymes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphoglycerate mutase, and phosphoglycerate kinase were identified in environmental metagenome-assembled genomes and were particularly prevalent within the Mimiviridae.
source: A genomic study using environmental metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), identified genes encoding the glycolytic enzymes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphoglycerate mutase, and phosphoglycerate kinase. These genes were considered to be particularly prevalent within the Mimiviridae (Figure 2A) and to a lesser extent in the Phycodnaviridae (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moniruzzaman et al., 2020 and Figure 2A

claim: Studies of Mimivirus metagenomes identified a unique protein domain architecture, with a single fused gene encoding the enzymes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and phosphoglycerate kinase.
source: Studies of Mimivirus metagenomes identified a unique protein domain architecture, with a single fused gene encoding the enzymes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and phosphoglycerate kinase, which serve in two adjacent steps in glycolysis (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moniruzzaman et al., 2020

claim: The fused gene architecture encoding glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and phosphoglycerate kinase is unique thus far.
source: Such protein architecture is unique thus far and may reflect a more efficient process for enzymatic activity.
evidence: Based on comparison with known protein architectures

claim: The fused gene architecture may reflect a more efficient process for enzymatic activity.
source: Such protein architecture is unique thus far and may reflect a more efficient process for enzymatic activity.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional implications of the unique architecture

claim: Three genes associated with gluconeogenesis were present in Mimiviridae genomes: fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and pyruvate carboxylase.
source: This same study revealed that three genes associated with gluconeogenesis were present in Mimiviridae genomes (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020): fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, which catalyzes the biotransformation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into fructose-6-phosphate; phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase that converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate; and pyruvate carboxylase that catalyzes the carboxylation of pyruvate to form oxaloacetate (Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moniruzzaman et al., 2020 and Figure 1, Table 1

claim: The presence of gluconeogenesis genes in infecting viruses suggests there could be reprogramming of the host glycolysis pathways.
source: The presence of such genes in infecting viruses also suggests there could be reprogramming of the host glycolysis pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of gluconeogenesis genes in viral genomes

claim: Fermentation is a heterotrophic anaerobic redox process that uses an organic compound as the terminal electron acceptor.
source: Fermentation is a heterotrophic anaerobic redox process that uses an organic compound as the terminal electron acceptor (Müller et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Müller et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2017

claim: Fermentation is considered as an ancient metabolic pathway.
source: It is considered as an ancient metabolic pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the evolutionary history of metabolic pathways

claim: Genes encoding for two key fermentation genes – pyruvate formate-lyase and pyruvate formate-lyase activating enzyme – have been found in Tetraselmis virus (TetV).
source: Genes encoding for two key fermentation genes – pyruvate formate-lyase and pyruvate formate-lyase activating enzyme – have been found in Tetraselmis virus (TetV) (Chlorodendrephycae) (Figure 1, Table 1), a mimivirus infecting the green algae Tetraselmis and land plants of the lineage Viridiplantae Müller et al., 2012.
evidence: Supported by citation to Müller et al., 2012 and Figure 1, Table 1

claim: The viral host of Tetraselmis virus utilizes anaerobic energy metabolism in low-oxygen conditions.
source: This viral host utilizes anaerobic energy metabolism in low-oxygen conditions, suggesting horizontal gene transfer (Müller et al., 2012; Schvarcz and Steward, 2018; T.-W. Sun et al., 2020, p. 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Müller et al., 2012; Schvarcz and Steward, 2018; T.-W. Sun et al., 2020

claim: Pyruvate formate-lyase catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate and coenzyme-A into formate and acetyl-CoA.
source: Pyruvate formate-lyase catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate and coenzyme-A into formate and acetyl-CoA (Knappe et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knappe et al., 1974

claim: In low oxygen conditions the host may use viral fermentation genes to generate the required energy via manipulation of anaerobic energy metabolism.
source: It is thought that in low oxygen conditions the host may use these viral genes to generate the required energy via manipulation of anaerobic energy metabolism.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the function of viral fermentation genes

claim: In anoxic conditions, the fermentation process may favor viral spreading, with the metabolism of infected cells being potentially maintained by virally encoded fermentation genes.
source: In the absence of light, algae and bacteria deplete dissolved oxygen in the superficial water. In anoxic conditions, the fermentation process thus may favor viral spreading, with the metabolism of infected cells being potentially maintained by virally encoded fermentation genes, an advantage for the viral host (Schvarcz and Steward, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schvarcz and Steward, 2018 and speculative reasoning

claim: Putative viral fermentation genes identified include mannitol 1-phosphate dehydrogenase and alpha-galactosidase in the Tetraselmis virus.
source: Other putative viral fermentation genes that have been identified include the mannitol metabolism protein, mannitol 1-phosphate dehydrogenase and the saccharide degradation enzyme alpha-galactosidase in the Tetraselmis virus (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by Table 1

claim: The role of mannitol 1-phosphate dehydrogenase and alpha-galactosidase genes in the Tetraselmis virus is less clear.
source: However, the role of these genes in the virus is less clear (Schvarcz and Steward, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schvarcz and Steward, 2018

claim: The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle is a linked series of biochemical reactions used by all aerobic organisms to release stored energy via the oxidation of acetyl-CoA.
source: The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle – also known as the Krebs cycle – is a linked series of biochemical reactions used by all aerobic organisms to release stored energy via the oxidation of acetyl-CoA, derived from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins (Smith and Morowitz, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith and Morowitz, 2004

claim: The TCA cycle is the central metabolic hub for many biochemical pathways.
source: It is the central metabolic hub for many biochemical pathways.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism

claim: The TCA cycle begins from acetate (in the form of acetyl-CoA) and water, to reduce NAD+ into NADH, with the concomitant release of carbon dioxide.
source: It begins from acetate (in the form of acetyl-CoA) and water, to reduce NAD +into NADH, with the concomitant release of carbon dioxide (Krebs and Johnson, 1937; Meléndez-Hevia et al., 1996; Noor et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krebs and Johnson, 1937; Meléndez-Hevia et al., 1996; Noor et al., 2010

claim: The NADH generated by the TCA cycle enters the oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport) pathway.
source: The NADH generated by this cycle enters the oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport) pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism

claim: As a result of the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, several molecules of ATP are produced.
source: As a result of these two closely linked metabolic pathways, several molecules of ATP are produced.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism

claim: Predicted TCA-related gene products were the most represented in MAGs studies, especially aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase, encoded in Mimiviridae and Phycodnaviridae genomes.
source: In the previously cited study based on MAGs, predicted TCA-related gene products were the most represented, especially aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase, encoded in Mimiviridae and Phycodnaviridae genomes (Moniruzzaman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moniruzzaman et al., 2020

claim: Aconitase was previously reported in Tupanvirus.
source: Aconitase was previously reported in Tupanvirus as well (Rodrigues et al., 2019; Figures 1 and 2.C Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodrigues et al., 2019 and Figures 1 and 2.C, Table 1

claim: In cells, aconitase catalyzes the stereospecific isomerization of citrate to isocitrate via cis-aconitate in a non-redox reaction.
source: In cells, aconitase catalyzes the stereospecific isomerization of citrate to isocitrate via cis-aconitate in a non-redox reaction.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of enzyme function

claim: Succinate dehydrogenase is a complex enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of succinate into fumarate, which generates electrons used to reduce oxygen into water.
source: Succinate dehydrogenase is a complex enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of succinate into fumarate, which generates electrons used to reduce oxygen into water (Oyedotun and Lemire, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oyedotun and Lemire, 2004

claim: The viral TCA enzymes may be utilized to boost host TCA cycle steps and hence energy production, possibly providing competitive advantages to the host.
source: The viral TCA enzymes may be utilized to boost host TCA cycle steps and hence energy production, possibly providing competitive advantages to the host.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the function of viral TCA enzymes

claim: Prymnesium kappa virus RF01 harbors six energy metabolism gene homologs.
source: The alga-infecting giant virus Prymnesium kappa virus RF01, which belongs to the Mimiviridae family, harbors six energy metabolism gene homologs (Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021

claim: Prymnesium kappa virus RF01 harbors the four succinate dehydrogenase subunits (A-D).
source: Among them, there are the four succinate dehydrogenase subunits (A-D), an enzyme involved in oxidative phosphorylation pathway and the TCA cycle (Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1, Table 1

claim: The gene encoding subunit A of succinate dehydrogenase is transcribed during Prymnesium kappa virus RF01 infection.
source: The gene encoding subunit A of this complex protein is transcribed during infection, again intimating that host energy metabolism could be modulated by the virus (Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021

claim: Putative succinate dehydrogenase genes detected by metatranscriptomic analysis were associated with Mimiviridae in surface oceanic waters of California.
source: Putative succinate dehydrogenase genes detected by metatranscriptomic analysis were associated with Mimiviridae, suggesting the gene product to be highly expressed in the virosphere of surface oceanic waters of California (USA) (Ha et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ha et al., 2021

claim: Succinate dehydrogenase may be widespread among marine Mimiviridae.
source: Putative succinate dehydrogenase genes detected by metatranscriptomic analysis were associated with Mimiviridae, suggesting the gene product to be highly expressed in the virosphere of surface oceanic waters of California (USA) (Ha et al., 2021), and may be widespread among marine Mimiviridae (Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021

claim: Malate synthase and isocitrate lyase were found expressed in different time points in viruses in the Mimiviridae.
source: In the same study, malate synthase and isocitrate lyase, other key enzymes of the TCA cycle, were found expressed in different time points in viruses in the Mimiviridae (Ha et al., 2021; Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ha et al., 2021 and Figure 1, Table 1

claim: Several predicted proteins in Pandoravirus massiliensis are homologues of enzymes involved in the TCA cycle: citrate synthase, aconitase, isocitrate/isopropyl malate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate decarboxylase, succinate dehydrogenase, and fumarase.
source: Several predicted proteins recently found in Pandoravirus massiliensis (Figure 2B) are homologues of enzymes involved in the TCA cycle, albeit with low % identities: citrate synthase, aconitase, isocitrate/isopropyl malate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate decarboxylase, succinate dehydrogenase, and fumarase (Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1, Figure 2B, Table 1

claim: The predicted isocitrate dehydrogenase of P. massiliensis was functional both in crude viral particles and following in vitro reconstitution of the purified recombinant protein.
source: The predicted isocitrate dehydrogenase of P. massiliensis was functional both in crude viral particles and following in vitro reconstitution of the purified recombinant protein.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing enzyme functionality

claim: P. massiliensis can generate an electrochemical gradient.
source: In addition, it was also demonstrated experimentally that P. massiliensis can generate an electrochemical gradient, an essential component of all living cells (Aherfi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aherfi et al., 2022 and experimental demonstration

claim: The membrane voltage in P. massiliensis may be involved in the amoeba infection process, notably in the early stages of infection.
source: The membrane voltage in P. massiliensis may be involved in the amoeba infection process, notably in the early stages of infection (Aherfi et al., 2022), helping the virus to release its DNA into host cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Aherfi et al., 2022 and speculative reasoning

source: Lipid metabolism consists of the catabolism of fatty acids and steroids/sterols in order to generate energy, and anabolic processes used to synthesize new lipids from smaller constituent molecules.

source: Lipidomic β-oxidation is the main metabolic pathway for the degradation of fatty acid molecules to generate acetyl-CoA, which then enters in the TCA cycle.

source: A recent metatranscriptomic time-series study from the California Current surface waters has identified many novel transcripts putatively for lipid metabolism enzymes in viruses in the Nucleocytoviricota.

claim: Identified viral genes included those predicted to be involved in lipid β-oxidation.
source: Identified viral genes included those predicted to be involved in lipid β-oxidation (Ha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ha et al., 2021

claim: Virus-mediated reprogramming of host central carbon metabolism is functional and occurs in oceanic surface waters.
